articles.title: [Comment] Adjuvant radiotherapy for atypical meningioma
articles.abstract: Surgical resection remains the mainstay of treatment for atypical meningiomas, corresponding to WHO grade 2 tumours, particularly given the substantial risk of recurrence after subtotal resection. Accordingly, adjuvant radiotherapy has been proposed as a means of reducing the risk of recurrence, and its role is relatively well accepted in patients with residual tumour. After gross total resection (defined as Simpson grade I–III), however, the rationale is less clear: 5-year progression-free survival with gross total resection alone is 67–86%, and the role of adjuvant radiotherapy remains controversial, with its benefit in disease control weighed against potential toxicities.

articles.title: [Correspondence] Taiwan's path to hepatitis C elimination
articles.abstract: WHO has established a global target to eliminate viral hepatitis as a public health threat by 2030.1 Chronic hepatitis C virus (HCV) infection remains one of the leading causes of cirrhosis, hepatocellular carcinoma, and liver-related mortality, affecting an estimated 50 million people worldwide.2 By integrating a comprehensive screening-to-cure cascade, HCV elimination has become an achievable public health goal.

articles.title: [Correspondence] How much can ASTRUM-006 tell us?
articles.abstract: Lin Shen and colleagues report improved event-free survival with perioperative serplulimab in PD-L1-positive resectable gastric or gastro-oesophageal junction adenocarcinoma.1 The trial is valuable: it selects patients by combined positive score and tests a chemotherapy-free adjuvant phase. However, we urge caution before it is read as practice-changing.

articles.title: [Correspondence] Colonoscopy screening and colorectal cancer outcomes: the NordICC trial
articles.abstract: Michal F Kaminski and colleagues report that colonoscopy screening reduced colorectal cancer incidence, but not mortality, during a 13-year follow-up.1 The response from the public health field will focus, as it always does, on mortality. We think this focus misses the point of the trial.

articles.title: [Correspondence] Colonoscopy screening and colorectal cancer outcomes: the NordICC trial – Authors’ reply
articles.abstract: We thank João Martins and Aneel Bhangu, Hermann Brenner and colleagues, and Uri Ladabaum and colleagues for their interesting comments on our report from the NordICC trial.1 We agree with Martins and Bhangu that colorectal cancer incidence is an interesting primary target for preventive screening tests, such as colonoscopy. The effect on cancer incidence is one of the advantages of preventive screening tests, compared with early detection screening tests (eg, breast cancer screening with mammography or prostate cancer screening with prostate-specific antigen).

articles.title: [Articles] Radiotherapy versus observation following surgical resection of WHO grade 2 atypical meningioma (ROAM/EORTC-1308): an international, multicentre, open-label, phase 3, randomised controlled trial
articles.abstract: Our findings suggest that adjuvant radiotherapy should be considered in patients with atypical meningioma after complete surgical resection of atypical meningioma when the prevention of recurrence is valued higher than the potential delayed adverse effects of radiotherapy. This practice will benefit patients by reducing meningioma recurrence. Decisions should be based on individual discussion with the patient.

articles.title: Colorectal Cancer Deaths Increase Among Younger Adults
articles.abstract: Deaths from most leading cancer types have decreased among individuals younger than 50 years, but deaths from colorectal cancer have increased, according to a research letter published in JAMA Network Open.

articles.title: “Pills You Can’t Stomach”: Poetry, Medicine, and Resisting Metaphor
articles.abstract: In most lyric poetry, of which “Pine, Arizona” is a fine example, such artful devices as metaphor are typically present. Yet when the lyric’s subject is medical, the poem can become an argument between beauty and reality. Lovely details, such as the fading colors of the evening sky and the ethereal singing of unseen coyotes, verge on metaphor yet resist its full embrace, as the spell is broken by a more unpoetic list of stark medical concerns: “The chemotherapy injections//you get in your abdomen. Pills you can’t stomach./Swelling from steroids. A frame irradiated,//and the ache of it all.” Thus the speaker struggles with whether even the impulse to make art can coexist with the blatant, bleak truths of a body wracked with pain and debilitated by both mortal illness and the adverse effects of its treatment. The longing for the possibility of healing through creative self-expression, suggested from the poem’s outset by the quiet pun of its title but never fully satisfied here, reminds us that even as poetry offers respite for many, still others wrestle with the limitations of aesthetic substitution. Still, importantly in this tortured lyric, the speaker never entirely gives up hope. In its conclusion, perhaps relief, and even survival, yet beckon: “…The hush of a forest leaning in to listen/to the sacredness of the living’s noise. You hear it?//There is enough yearning/to get us into tomorrow.”

articles.title: [Editorial] Microplastics and cancer: a looming threat?
articles.abstract: Microplastics are a growing global concern and have been linked to various health conditions. A study presented by Ilias Dimeas and colleagues at the 2026 European Respiratory Society conference found a higher burden of microplastics in the lungs of patients with lung cancer than in those without cancer. In the study, 70% of 100 people undergoing a bronchoscopy had detectable microplastics in at least one sample, and patients with lung cancer were more likely to have detectable microplastics in their samples than patients without lung cancer.

articles.title: [Comment] Exercise oncology: from trials and guidelines to routine clinical care
articles.abstract: In oncology practice, there are trade-offs between quality of life and survival for many therapies. Similar trade-offs exist for drug reimbursement based on therapeutic effectiveness, affected population, and cost.

articles.title: [Comment] Looking at cancer burden in Africa through a new lens
articles.abstract: Cancer remains a leading cause of death and disability globally, with a disproportionate rising burden in Africa.1,2 Effective policy response has been consistently hampered by fragmented and incomplete cancer surveillance data.3 For a long time, there has been an assumption that a global uniform framework for understanding cancer risk factors exists and is applicable universally.4 This concept of harmonised global data is plausible in well structured and well resourced health systems in which research and care systems are integrated—systems that exist mostly in high-income regions.

articles.title: [Comment] Personalised medicine in oncology: inequality aversion in a fast-moving field
articles.abstract: Personalised medicine has been shown to improve patient care and holds promise to further benefit treatment results. The Lancet Oncology Commission on accelerating equitable cancer genomics and precision oncology in health care and research provides an overview of state-of-the-art treatments and the situation in low-income and middle-income countries (LMICs). From targeted treatment using companion diagnostics, identifying targets to guide treatment decisions, to broad ‘omics testing in cancer of unknown primary and metastasised tumours, the field is vast and inequalities exist within and between countries.

articles.title: [Comment] Ethical priorities in global cancer genomics and precision oncology
articles.abstract: Amid the promise of cancer genomics and precision oncology lies complex and ethically weighty issues. Genomics and other ‘omics are undoubtedly transforming cancer care for thousands of patients annually, enabling better prognosis, access to treatments or trials, or informing relatives. Yet, these interventions overwhelmingly benefit people in high-income countries: they are failing to reach most patients with cancer who could benefit, and those who are reached could, for reasons including health system readiness or data representation and interpretation, receive no or marginal benefit to their care.

articles.title: [Comment] Inequities in access to precision oncology: shared challenges, unified blueprint
articles.abstract: Precision oncology has substantially changed the therapeutic landscape from a “one size fits all” approach to that of individualised (or personalised) treatments.1 The promise of precision oncology extends across the entire cancer continuum from prevention, early diagnosis, subtyping of tumours, treatment selection, risk-adapted therapies, development of novel anticancer medicines, and post-treatment surveillance.2 The Lancet Oncology Commission on accelerating equitable cancer genomics and precision oncology in health care and research focuses on the current challenges and practical solutions to faciliate wider implementation.

articles.title: [Comment] Beyond the evidence: why multistakeholder cooperation will determine whether cancer genomics reaches patients
articles.abstract: The Lancet Oncology Commission on accelerating equitable cancer genomics and precision oncology presents a worrying picture.1 While the number of precision oncology drugs continues to increase,2,3 access to testing and matched therapies remains profoundly unequal, research is concentrated in high-income countries (HICs) and populations of European ancestry, and expanding testing capacity has not always translated into proportionate population-level benefit. The Commission's survey of national cancer control programmes (NCCPs), conducted in collaboration with the Union for International Cancer Control and WHO International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC) across 34 countries, found partial integration of genomics into most NCCPs, including in HICs.

articles.title: [Comment] Ecological neglect: critical oversight in precision oncology governance
articles.abstract: The Lancet Oncology Commission on accelerating equitable cancer genomics and precision oncology in health care and research1 examines the gap between the promise of precision oncology and its delivery across global health systems. Raffaella Casolino and colleagues argue that precision oncology has advanced with remarkable speed, yet its clinical impact and sustainability remain uneven, meaning that for much of the world, precision oncology remains just a promise. The authors argue that if the vision of precision oncology is to be realised, health systems need to generate, integrate, govern, and learn from data.

articles.title: [Comment] Affordability in the era of precision oncology
articles.abstract: Cancer drugs are increasingly unaffordable for health systems. Global spending on cancer drugs will reach US$441 billion by 2029.1 This 75% increase over 5 years cannot be explained by population ageing or changing prevalence alone. Instead, the price of cancer drugs is driving accelerated spending growth.2 Rising prices place considerable pressure on health systems, particularly when increased spending is not matched by commensurate improvements in patient health. Unfortunately, many expensive cancer drugs have highly uncertain safety and efficacy evidence at the time of market authorisation.

articles.title: [Comment] Counting who was not tested: artificial intelligence extraction of genomic and treatment data from hospital records
articles.abstract: The Lancet Oncology Commission on accelerating equitable access to cancer genomics and precision oncology provides an important framework defining indicators that health systems can and should measure.1 Operationalising these indicators, however, requires substantial data infrastructure. One indicator in the Commission's Precision Oncology Access Cascade defines the group of eligible patients who receive recommended genomic testing. The number of patients tested is relatively straightforward to obtain; however, the number meeting the guideline criteria is not because this information is usually recorded as unstructured narrative text rather than as a structured field.

articles.title: [Comment] Blank spaces on the map: genomics for global cancer research
articles.abstract: For most of the history of cancer genomics, the map of our knowledge has had blank spaces on it. In the Pan-Cancer Analysis of Whole Genomes, for example, roughly three quarters of donors were of European descent; samples from Latin American donors made up only about 1% of the large public repositories and samples from patients of Middle Eastern descent were almost entirely absent.1

articles.title: [Comment] England's National Cancer Plan; ambition without accountability
articles.abstract: Publication of England's National Cancer Control Plan (NCCP) in February, 2026,1 marked a hard-won achievement, after years of advocacy from patients, clinicians, charities, parliamentarians, and The Lancet Oncology.2,3 The expectation was to address long-standing systemic issues in treatment delays and quality, workforce shortages, and inequalities; but hopes were quickly dashed.4 The plan had no real new money, no additional workforce capacity, no expansion of treatment infrastructure, no prioritisation, and no implementation strategy.

articles.title: [Correspondence] Re-evaluating aglatimagene in localised prostate cancer
articles.abstract: We read with great interest the Article by Theodore L DeWeese and colleagues detailing the results of the PrTK03 phase 3 trial, which evaluated the addition of aglatimagene besadenovec (CAN-2409) and valacyclovir to standard-of-care external beam radiation therapy (EBRT) for localised prostate cancer.1 We commend the investigators for executing this decade-spanning study. The biological premise—using an adenoviral vector to exert localised cytotoxicity of a systemically administered prodrug while stimulating a T-cell-mediated immune response—is scientifically sound.

articles.title: [Correspondence] Re-evaluating aglatimagene in localised prostate cancer – Authors' reply
articles.abstract: We thank Thomas Büttner and colleagues for their interest in our Article on the PrTK03 trial.1 In our trial, disease-free survival was the prospectively specified, US Food and Drug Administration-agreed primary endpoint under a Special Protocol Assessment, analysed in the intention-to-treat population and defined to include local failure, including positive biopsy, regional failure, distant metastasis, or death.1 The US Food and Drug Administration did not agree to use biochemical failure as a disease-free survival event.

articles.title: [Correspondence] Proton pump inhibitors and durvalumab in PACIFIC
articles.abstract: Leonardo Brunetti and colleagues’ post-hoc analysis of the PACIFIC trial in The Lancet Oncology addresses an important and clinically timely question: whether baseline exposure to proton pump inhibitors or antibiotics modifies the benefit of durvalumab after concurrent chemoradiotherapy in patients with unresectable stage III non-small-cell lung cancer.1 The observed association between proton pump inhibitor exposure and inferior progression-free and overall survival in the durvalumab group, but not in the placebo group, is thought provoking.

articles.title: [Correspondence] Proton pump inhibitors and durvalumab in PACIFIC – Authors' reply
articles.abstract: We thank our colleagues for their thoughtful comments on our post-hoc analysis of PACIFIC.1 Their correspondence raises two issues: the definition of survival events and whether proton pump inhibitor exposure is causal or reflects its prescribing context.

articles.title: [News] Trump cuts childhood vaccine recommendations
articles.abstract: The US President Donald Trump has issued an executive order stressing “maximal parental choice” and cutting the number of childhood vaccines recommended by the federal government to 11 from 18.

articles.title: [News] Nigeria plans major expansion of radiotherapy capacity
articles.abstract: Africa's most populous country Nigeria plans to procure and install 35 additional linear accelerators (LINACs), substantially expanding its radiotherapy capacity. Six Cancer Centres of Excellence are also being developed, with centres in Katsina, Enugu, and Benin completed and commissioned. However, the new machines translating into wider access depends on availability of specialist staffing, maintenance, financing, and where the additional capacity is located.

articles.title: [News] Delays in cancer referrals and care lead to harm and missed diagnoses in England
articles.abstract: Late and missed diagnoses, delays in cancer care, and physical harm were partly caused by England's National Health Service (NHS) system for general practitioners (GPs) seeking specialist advice before patient referral to hospital, according to an investigation by the Health Services Safety Investigations Body (HSSIB).

articles.title: [News] Increased tobacco production and cigarette imports in Africa
articles.abstract: While tobacco-leaf production across the world declined by 19% between 2012 and 2024, it increased by 9% in Africa, according to a WHO analysis published on Aug 31, 2026. Moreover, during this period, there was a more than two-times increase in cigarette imports to Africa—from US$833 million to $1·77 billion.

articles.title: [News] 2026 World Conference on Lung Cancer
articles.abstract: Interim results from the phase 3 ARTEMIS-008 trial, presented by Jie Wang (Chinese Academy of Medical Sciences, Beijing, China), suggest risvutatug rezetecan, a B7-H3-directed antibody–drug conjugate (ADC), could be the new standard of care in relapsed small-cell lung cancer (SCLC). Patients were randomly assigned (1:1) to receive risvutatug rezetecan (8·0 mg/kg; n=230) or topotecan (1·2 mg/m2 on days 1–5; n=231) every 3 weeks. At a median follow-up of 12·2 months, overall survival (the primary endpoint) was significantly improved with risvutatug rezetecan compared with topotecan (18·5 vs 10·3 months; HR 0·46 [95% CI 0·35–0·62).

articles.title: [News] Kenya agrees major cuts to cancer drug prices
articles.abstract: The Kenyan Government has agreed a deal with Pfizer that could reduce the price of selected cancer medicines by seven times. Costs are expected to drop from as much as 1 million Kenyan Shillings (KSh; US$7725) to below KSh50 000 ($386) per treatment cycle for some drugs. The agreement covers nine cancers: breast, stomach, colorectal, lung, prostate, and oesophageal cancers, as well as leukaemia, lymphoma, and multiple myeloma.

articles.title: [News] Toxic dust around the World Trade Center
articles.abstract: On Sept 8, 2026, New York City authorities released more than 170 000 pages of documents showing that officials misled the public about toxic air quality levels after the Sept 11, 2001, attack that killed more than 2600 people at the World Trade Center (WTC). Health researchers say the documents contain little medical information that is new but confirm that carcinogens and toxins were present months after the attacks, exposing 400 000 people in lower Manhattan to smoke, dust, and combustion products.

articles.title: [Perspectives] Cancer's new anxiety: not a death sentence, but delay
articles.abstract: Throughout the history of cancer research, hyperbole has never been in short supply—whether it be Richard Nixon's war, Joe Biden's moonshot, or Cancer Research UK's 2023 declaration of a golden era. Driving such rhetoric has been the need to act against an enduring societal concern—cancer, the so-called Big C, society's number one fear.

articles.title: [Perspectives] Against cancer, not against dying: Ernest Becker in the oncology clinic
articles.abstract: When American cultural anthropologist Ernest Becker was awarded the 1974 Pulitzer Prize for his book, The Denial of Death, he had died of colorectal cancer only 2 months earlier. More than half a century later, the book feels almost uncomfortably contemporary in the oncology clinic. Although the book does not address cancer care directly, it speaks to what cancer reveals: mortality, and the symbolic structures we build to make that knowledge bearable. For Becker, identities, professions, institutions, religions, families, reputations, and achievements are ways in which the fragile self seeks continuity beyond finitude.

articles.title: [Perspectives] Sir Chris Hoy's Tour de 4 charity cycle ride returns
articles.abstract: Mention the name Chris Hoy and it's natural to picture the Olympic cyclist, who won six gold medals and one silver in Sydney, Athens, Beijing, and London between 2000 and 2012. Fans voted for him to be named as the BBC Sports Personality of the Year in 2008, and he was knighted by the late Queen Elizabeth in the 2009 New Year honours list. However, over the past 2 years, Hoy has become famous for a completely different reason. In October, 2024, he revealed that he had received a terminal diagnosis of stage-4 prostate cancer, which had spread to his bones.

articles.title: [Perspectives] Differing approaches to cancer at the Edinburgh Fringe
articles.abstract: “I had cancer a couple of years ago—I don’t like to talk about it,” grinned comedian Matt Forde during his show at the Edinburgh Festival Fringe, the world's largest arts festival, which took place in Edinburgh, UK, on Aug 7–31, 2026. With a sly grin at his audience, he added “I’m not going to use it to sell tickets for another sold out night in Edinburgh.” Forde, who is best known for his impressions of politicians, was diagnosed in July, 2023, with a chordoma, a very rare sarcoma at the base of his spine.

articles.title: [Articles] Chemotherapy with or without pembrolizumab followed by maintenance pembrolizumab with or without olaparib as first-line treatment of patients with advanced BRCA non-mutated epithelial ovarian cancer (ENGOT-OV43/GOG-3036/KEYLYNK-001): a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled, phase 3 trial
articles.abstract: Pembrolizumab plus chemotherapy followed by maintenance with pembrolizumab–olaparib showed a statistically significant and clinically meaningful improvement in progression-free survival versus chemotherapy, suggesting that this regimen might have potential for patients with newly diagnosed BRCA non-mutated stage III–IV epithelial ovarian cancer.

articles.title: [Articles] Global burden of cancer attributable to infections in 2024: a worldwide incidence analysis
articles.abstract: Our findings highlight the importance of infection control to achieve cancer prevention. Scientifically proven, but often underused, approaches include HPV and HBV vaccination; testing and treatment of HIV, H pylori, HBV, and HCV; safe injection practices; access to condoms and pre-exposure prophylaxis to prevent HIV transmission; and screening of precancerous lesions for HPV-driven cervical and anal cancer. Our findings also inform the investment cases for research and development for new prevention tools, most notably for EBV.

articles.title: [Articles] Hypofractionated versus conventional fractionated postmastectomy radiotherapy for patients with high-risk breast cancer (CHN HYPOPMRT): 10-year outcomes from a randomised, non-inferiority, open-label, phase 3 trial
articles.abstract: Hypofractionated postmastectomy radiotherapy provided durable locoregional control with no increase in severe late adverse events compared with conventional fractionation, supporting its use as a more time-efficient option than conventional fractionated radiotherapy.

articles.title: [Articles] Patient-reported symptom monitoring in patients with lung cancer (SYMPRO-Lung trial): long-term, post-hoc survival results of a multicentre, stepped-wedged, cluster-randomised clinical trial
articles.abstract: Weekly PRO symptom monitoring was associated with meaningful improvement in long-term overall survival among patients with stage I–IV lung cancer. Median overall survival was 5 months longer in the intervention group than in the control group. These findings underscore the value of implementing PRO symptom monitoring within routine care for patients with lung cancer.

articles.title: [Articles] An integrated lifestyle intervention for mitigation of adverse effects associated with androgen deprivation therapy for prostate cancer (STAMINA): a multicentre, randomised trial
articles.abstract: The STAMINA lifestyle intervention meets best practice guidelines, can be implemented in NHS trusts in England, and offers clinicians a clear basis for identification and prescription of a supervised exercise and dietary advice intervention to mitigate negative effects associated with ADT.

articles.title: [Articles] Development and external validation of a new prognostic model for metastatic clear cell renal cell carcinoma: a preregistered analysis using data from randomised clinical trials in the checkpoint inhibitor era
articles.abstract: The CPI2 model, using 14 readily available clinical parameters, demonstrated improvement in discriminative accuracy compared with the IMDC model. This classification should be further validated in other trial and observational populations and be used to reanalyse heterogeneity of treatment effects of immune checkpoint inhibitor-based combination regimens in trials shaping the current and future treatment landscape.

articles.title: [Articles] Long-term exposure to wildfire-related PM2·5 and overall survival of older patients with lung cancer: a retrospective, registry-based cohort study
articles.abstract: Wildfire-related PM2·5 showed greater toxicity per unit exposure than non-wildfire PM2·5. As wildfire-related PM2·5 is the fastest-growing contributor to ambient air pollution, there is an urgent need for updated strategies to manage wildfires and mitigate their effects.

articles.title: [Articles] Burden of cancer in Africa, 1990–2023: a systematic analysis from the Global Burden of Disease Study 2023
articles.abstract: Cancer is a growing contributor to the disease burden in Africa, with rising cases, deaths, and DALYs disproportionately affecting children, adolescents, and young adults. The increase in age-standardised mortality and DALY rates stands in sharp contrast to the ambitions of the Sustainable Development Goals for 2030 and the African Union Agenda 2063. Addressing this burden will require coordinated national and international action, with health-system strengthening and context-specific cancer-control strategies spanning prevention, early diagnosis, and treatment.

articles.title: [The Lancet Oncology Commission] Accelerating equitable cancer genomics and precision oncology in health care and research: a Lancet Oncology Commission
articles.abstract: Cancer genomics and precision oncology are increasingly central to cancer care, but many health systems struggle to implement them equitably, effectively, and sustainably. This Commission defines the current global precision oncology landscape and analyses the scientific, structural, and health-system challenges shaping its delivery and impact. Findings indicate that access to cancer genomics and precision oncology remains profoundly unequal across and within countries, leaving millions of patients without guideline-indicated interventions each year.

articles.title: [Clinical Picture] Not all thoracic micronodules are metastases
articles.abstract: A 58-year-old female, lifelong non-smoker with history of Parkinson's disease, presented with a palpable right breast lump to the Odette Cancer Centre at Sunnybrook Health and Sciences Centre (Toronto, ON, Canada) in April, 2024, and was diagnosed with right-sided oestrogen receptor-positive, HER2-positive breast cancer (cT3N0). She received neoadjuvant dose dense doxorubicin–cyclophosphamide followed by paclitaxel, trastuzumab, and pertuzumab. Lumpectomy and sentinel lymph node biopsy was performed revealing a pathological complete response.

articles.title: Molecular residual disease: Charting a new path for treating resectable solid tumors
articles.abstract: Molecular residual disease (MRD), detected via circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) after curative-intent surgery, identifies resectable solid tumor patients at high recurrence risk, thereby enabling enriched trials with larger effect sizes and smaller samples. Yet enrichment narrows the eligible population and thus challenges conventional randomized designs. We propose an MRD Registry as an external control cohort that integrates quantitative ctDNA data with outcomes to validate ctDNA dynamics as response indicators—facilitating efficient MRD-based trial design and accelerating novel therapy development.

articles.title: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma: The Vision of Heracles
articles.abstract: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) remains among the deadliest malignancies, as tumors evolve faster than therapies. Resistance is ecological, not merely KRAS driven, involving overlooked players like high-grade pancreatic intraepithelial neoplasias (PanINs), peripancreatic fat, stromal mechanics, myeloid-neural circuits, metabolic rewiring, and systemic host responses. We propose precision interception targeting PanIN/intraductal papillary mucinous neoplasm (IPMN) biology, spatial-functional-proteogenomic classification beyond transcriptomics, the Heracles Protocol (measure, prime, strike, and adapt), and integrated technologies from AI pathology to exosomal delivery and CRISPR-based synergy mapping, together making PDAC more tractable.

articles.title: Latent tumor killers awakened
articles.abstract: In this issue of Cancer Cell, Kehl et al. construct a single-cell atlas of bone marrow T cells from patients with bone marrow-resident malignancies, identifying tumor-reactive populations existing in a state of latent competence. A 15-gene signature identifies this subset, which is expanded by immunotherapies and predicts clinical responses.

articles.title: Scherer’s map, remapped
articles.abstract: Scherer’s century-old classification of expansive and infiltrative glioma growth remains foundational to neuro-oncology. In this issue of Cancer Cell, Hoefflin et al. use spatial RNA and protein profiling of IDH-mutant gliomas to reveal hypoxia and necrosis as organizing centers of expansive growth and white-matter tracts as guides and constraints on invasion.

articles.title: Tumor-infiltrating plasma cell targets as a source for immunotherapies
articles.abstract: Tumor-infiltrating plasma cells are key responders to immunotherapy. In this issue of Cancer Cell, Meyerhoff et al. show that plasma cells from lung lesions of anti-PD-1-treated patients target citrullinated proteins. Engineering CAR T cells with these plasma cells scFv reveals anti-tumor specificity without adverse effects, identifying therapeutic opportunities.

articles.title: TIME in motion: How response takes shape
articles.abstract: Biomarkers for immune checkpoint inhibitors have largely treated the tumor immune microenvironment as a fixed property. In this issue of Cancer Cell, Lin et al. assemble a longitudinal pan-cancer single-cell atlas and show that the direction of immune-state remodeling during therapy is more informative than baseline composition.

articles.title: Tumor evolution shapes metastatic competence in colorectal cancer
articles.abstract: In this issue of Cancer Cell, Manca et al. investigate the genomic evolution and metastatic tropism of over 7,000 colorectal cancers. Integrating primary tumor location, genomic alterations, and clinical variables, they reveal how distinct patterns of tumor evolution shape metastatic competence and impact organ tropism, offering a framework to refine surveillance.

articles.title: EGFR-targeting ADCs: From oncogene addiction to antigen-guided drug delivery
articles.abstract: In this issue of Cancer Cell, Li et al. report a first-in-human phase 1 study of SYS6010, an epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR)-targeting antibody-drug conjugate, in advanced solid tumors. The study highlights how EGFR-directed therapy moves beyond kinase inhibition toward antigen-guided cytotoxic delivery in non-small cell lung cancer.

articles.title: Biological aging and the hidden architecture of early-onset cancer risk
articles.abstract: Across birth cohorts, in a Nature Medicine study, Tian et al. identify larger biological age gaps associated with early-onset lung, colorectal, and uterine cancers across birth cohorts. These findings position biological age as an integrative marker of physiological dysregulation. Future work combining aging clocks and mutational signatures could distinguish tumor-promoting states from tumor-initiating exposures.

articles.title: Integrated clinicogenomic analysis reveals the evolution and metastatic tropisms of advanced colorectal cancer
articles.abstract: Manca et al. analyze >7,000 colorectal cancers, integrating next-generation sequencing and clinical data. They define tumor genomics, clonality and dosage of mutations, and metastatic tropisms and their effects on patient outcomes. Incorporating metastatic sites, primary tumor location, and genomics, they develop an organ-specific risk model for metastasis.

articles.title: A stress-adaptive lipid kinase axis defines metabolic vulnerabilities in neuroendocrine prostate cancer
articles.abstract: Zheng et al. identify a PIKfyve-ER stress-lipogenesis axis that enables neuroendocrine prostate cancer cells to tolerate elevated basal ER stress through PIKfyve-dependent lysosomal homeostasis and SREBP-driven lipogenesis. Dual inhibition of PIKfyve and FASN disrupts these adaptive pathways, driving terminal UPR activation and apoptosis and providing a robust translational strategy.

articles.title: Latent effector T cells mediate immunotherapy responses in the bone marrow microenvironment
articles.abstract: Kehl et al. characterize tumor-reactive T cells in the bone marrow of patients with multiple myeloma and AML. These cells adopt an effector state distinct from exhausted solid tumor TILs. The TFiT classifier stratifies immunotherapy, but not chemotherapy, response, identifying a latent, therapeutically engageable anti-tumor compartment.

articles.title: Depletion of an immature cord blood NK subset reverses trogocytosis-driven CAR NK dysfunction
articles.abstract: Li et al. identify a previously unrecognized NK cell subset that limits cord blood-derived CAR-NK cell therapy by diverting tumor targeting and promoting self-directed fratricide and show that donor cell composition shapes efficacy while offering a practical manufacturing strategy to improve consistency, persistence, and antitumor activity of off-the-shelf CAR-NK therapies.

articles.title: Tumor-infiltrating plasma cell profiling after PD-1 blockade reveals tumor-specific antibodies
articles.abstract: Meyerhoff et al. identify tumor-infiltrating plasma cells as a source of antibodies with therapeutic potential. Their lead antibody, PC-1, recognizes citrullinated antigens on cancer and tumor-promoting myeloid cells and can be repurposed to guide CAR T cell therapy.

articles.title: SYS6010, epidermal growth factor receptor-targeting antibody-drug conjugate for advanced non-small cell lung cancer: A phase 1 trial
articles.abstract: Li et al. report results from a first-in-human study showing that SYS6010, an EGFR-targeted antibody-drug conjugate, demonstrates encouraging antitumor activity with a tolerable safety profile in pretreated advanced NSCLC, providing evidence that warrants further clinical development.

articles.title: Tumor immune microenvironment remodeling predicts response to checkpoint inhibitor therapy
articles.abstract: Lin et al. assemble a longitudinal pan-cancer single-cell atlas that tracks how the tumor immune microenvironment remodels during checkpoint inhibitor therapy. They show that the direction of remodeling, rather than the pre-treatment state, predicts response and translate these dynamics into a baseline gene signature that forecasts outcome across cancer types.

articles.title: A self-amplifying nerve-fibroblast circuit drives colorectal cancer progression
articles.abstract: Kobayashi et al. demonstrate that cholinergic signaling induces NTN1 secretion from colorectal CAFs, which in turn enhances intratumoral cholinergic innervation. Increased acetylcholine and CAF-derived NTN1 then accelerate cancer cell growth through tumoral CHRM3 and UNC5B. Blocking CHRM3 or NTN1 may represent a promising therapeutic approach for CRC.

articles.title: Spatial analysis reveals the evolving organization of IDH-mutant glioma
articles.abstract: Hoefflin et al. define organizational principles of IDH-mutant gliomas using multimodal spatial profiling. They identify three spatial archetypes across histological grades and reveal that brain anatomy and hypoxia represent distinct spatial organizing forces, with the white-gray matter junction acting as a functional barrier to invasion.

articles.title: Effect of Screening with Multicancer Early-Detection Test on Late-Stage Cancer Diagnosis.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Whether screening with blood-based early-detection tests for multiple cancers in addition to usual care has clinical utility is unknown. METHODS: In a randomized, controlled trial conducted in England, we obtained peripheral blood from persons 50 to 77 years of age at up to three annual visits. After baseline blood collection, participants were randomly assigned in a 1:1 ratio to the intervention group (participants whose blood was tested) or the control group (participants whose blood was stored). Participants and trial personnel were initially unaware of the group assignments. The primary end point was stage III or IV cancer among 12 prespecified types of cancer, and a key secondary end point was stage IV cancer among the 12 prespecified types. The differences between the groups in the incidence rate (the number of first eligible events divided by person-years at risk) were measured after three screening rounds and at least 12 months of follow-up after the last participant's third visit. RESULTS: Overall, 71,122 participants were randomly assigned to the intervention group and 71,128 to the control group. The incidence rate of stage III or IV cancer (primary end point) did not differ significantly between the groups (incidence rate ratio [intervention vs. control], 1.03; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.92 to 1.14, P = 0.63). The incidence rate ratio for stage IV cancer (a key secondary end point) after 3 screening rounds was 0.86 (95% CI, 0.74 to 1.00). Less than 1% of participants had trial-related adverse events; none were serious. CONCLUSIONS: In this trial, we did not observe a lower incidence rate of stage III or IV cancers across 12 prespecified cancers after three screening rounds with multicancer early-detection testing plus usual care than with usual care alone. Further follow-up is warranted to assess the way in which findings for stage III or IV cancers and the between-group difference in stage IV cancers evolve over time. (Funded by Grail; NHS-Galleri ClinicalTrials.gov number, NCT05611632; ISRCTN number, ISRCTN91431511.).

articles.title: Stool-based methylated syndecan-2 test and fecal immunochemical test for advanced colorectal neoplasia screening in the Chinese population: A multicenter randomized noncomparative study.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Colorectal cancer (CRC) is among the most prevalent malignancies, with an increasing incidence in China, posing increasing challenges to current screening strategies. This study aimed to evaluate the feasibility of a screening strategy based on the stool-based methylated Syndecan-2 gene (mSDC2) test for detecting advanced colorectal neoplasia in the Chinese population. METHODS: In this multicenter randomized study, participants aged 45-80 years and identified through community screening were randomized to take either the mSDC2 test or a fecal immunochemical test (FIT), and those with positive results were referred for colonoscopy between 2020 and 2022. The primary outcome was the detection rate of advanced colorectal neoplasia, including advanced adenoma, advanced serrated polyps, and CRC. The secondary outcome was adherence to colonoscopy. Univariable and multivariable logistic regression analyses were conducted to evaluate colonoscopy adherence among participants with positive stool-based test results. RESULTS: A total of 44,475 eligible participants were enrolled from 189 communities (93 in the mSDC2 test group and 96 in the FIT group). In the mSDC2 test group ( n = 21,854), the detection rate of advanced neoplasia was 0.53% ( n = 115), including 93 (0.43%) advanced adenomas, 8 (0.04%) advanced serrated polyps, and 17 (0.08%) CRC cases. In the FIT group ( n = 22,621), the detection rate of advanced neoplasia was 0.47% ( n = 106), including 71 (0.31%) advanced adenomas, 9 (0.04%) advanced serrated polyps, and 29 (0.13%) CRC cases. In addition, adherence to colonoscopy was greater in the mSDC2 test group (35.6% vs. 26.4%; odds ratio: 1.59, 95% confidence interval: 1.36-1.87; P <0.001). CONCLUSIONS: This study revealed the effectiveness of the mSDC2 test and FIT in detecting advanced colorectal neoplasia in a large Chinese population in a real-world setting, and indicated a possible improvement in adherence to colonoscopy for the mSDC2 test. Further studies with improved comparability and longer follow-up are warranted to clarify its clinical utility. REGISTRATION: ClinicalTrials.gov , No. NCT04221854.

articles.title: Older adults with resectable gastric cancer undergoing perioperative chemotherapy or preoperative chemoradiotherapy plus perioperative chemotherapy: A secondary analysis of the AGITG TOPGEAR phase III trial.
articles.abstract: PURPOSE: To evaluate treatment adherence, adverse events, and survival in older (≥70 years) adults undergoing perioperative treatment for gastric cancer. METHODS: Patients with resectable gastric/gastro-esophageal junction adenocarcinoma (ECOG 0-1) enrolled in the phase III TOPGEAR trial were randomized to perioperative chemotherapy (ECF/ECX or FLOT) alone or perioperative chemotherapy plus preoperative chemoradiotherapy (45 Gy in 25 fractions with concurrent fluoropyrimidine). In this exploratory analysis, treatment completion, grade ≥ 3 adverse events (CTCAE v3.0), surgical outcomes, overall survival (OS) and progression-free survival (PFS) were compared between older and younger adults. RESULTS: Of the 574 patients enrolled, 135 (24%) were ≥ 70 years. Older adults more frequently required preoperative chemotherapy dose reductions, omissions, or delays (chemoradiotherapy: 55% vs 35%, p = 0.004; chemotherapy: 60% vs 48%, p = 0.087). Rates of grade ≥ 3 adverse events were comparable between older and younger patients (chemoradiotherapy: 66% vs 67%, p = 0.874; chemotherapy: 68% vs 59%, p = 0.220), but older adults more often had hematologic toxicity and grade ≥ 3 diarrhea in the chemotherapy group (56% vs 37%, p = 0.006; 21% vs 6%, p < 0.001). Resection rates, grade 3/4 surgical complications, number of removed lymph nodes, and 30-/90-day mortality were similar by age. OS and PFS were comparable across age groups, with numerically favorable outcomes for older adults (OS: HR 0.86, 95% CI 0.58-1.26 [chemoradiotherapy]; HR 0.75, 95% CI 0.51-1.11 [chemotherapy]; PFS: HR 0.78, 95% CI 0.53-1.15 [chemoradiotherapy]; HR 0.70, 95% CI 0.47-1.03 [chemotherapy]). CONCLUSIONS: Older adults with gastric cancer achieved comparable oncologic outcomes to younger patients, despite more frequent treatment modifications and higher hematologic toxicity.

articles.title: Association of serum uric acid with circulating inflammatory proteins and treatment response to ixekizumab in patients with psoriasis: A multicenter prospective cohort study in China.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Serum uric acid (SUA) has been implicated in various inflammatory conditions, yet its association with inflammatory proteins and treatment outcomes in psoriasis remains unclear. This study aimed to investigate the association of SUA levels with specific circulating inflammatory proteins and treatment response to ixekizumab, a monoclonal antibody against interleukin-17A, in patients with moderate-to-severe psoriasis. METHODS: Patients attending 26 dermatology centers across China were recruited into this real-world prospective cohort study conducted between August 2020 and May 2022. The SUA levels of the participants were measured to assess hyperuricemia, and treatment response was evaluated using the Psoriasis Area and Severity Index (PASI). All participants received ixekizumab at a dose of 160 mg at week 0, followed by 80 mg every 2 weeks through week 12. Adjusted logistic regression analysis was used to explore differences in treatment response between patients with and without hyperuricemia. The restricted cubic spline (RCS) was employed to explore the continuous relationship between SUA and the response outcomes. Specifically, we measured 92 circulating plasma inflammatory markers using the Olink Proteomics. RESULTS: A total of 390 patients with psoriasis were included in the study. The psoriasis patients with hyperuricemia demonstrated a higher prevalence of obesity, hyperlipidemia, and hyperglycemia compared with those without hyperuricemia. After 12 weeks of ixekizumab treatment, patients with hyperuricemia exhibited a lower likelihood of achieving PASI 75 (adjusted odds ratio [aOR] 0.84, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.69-0.99), PASI 90 (aOR 0.37, 95% CI 0.15-0.62), and PASI 100 (aOR 0.57, 95% CI 0.37-0.91). Olink Proteomics identified significant correlations between SUA concentration and the levels of 26 circulating inflammatory proteins, and pathway analysis showed enrichment of pathways such as response to tumor necrosis factor (TNF), lymphocyte activation, and cytokine activity. CONCLUSION: Elevated SUA levels can hinder the effectiveness of ixekizumab and positively correlate with specific circulating inflammatory proteins in patients with psoriasis, emphasizing the need for further investigation and consideration of metabolic factors in psoriasis management strategies. TRIAL REGISTERATION: Chinese Clinical Trial Registry (ChiCTR2000036186).

articles.title: Radiotherapy versus observation following surgical resection of WHO grade 2 atypical meningioma (ROAM/EORTC-1308): an international, multicentre, open-label, phase 3, randomised controlled trial.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: WHO grade 2 atypical meningioma is a primary brain tumour with a high risk of recurrence even after complete surgical resection. The role of adjuvant radiotherapy remains uncertain. We aimed to assess whether adjuvant radiotherapy reduces recurrence compared with observation in patients with a newly diagnosed atypical meningioma who have undergone complete surgical resection. METHODS: ROAM/EORTC-1308 was an international, multicentre, open-label, phase 3, randomised controlled trial, conducted at 58 hospitals and academic centres in 11 countries. Eligible sites had appropriate multidisciplinary expertise, neurosurgery, and radiotherapy facilities. Patients aged 16 years or older who had undergone a surgeon-assessed complete surgical resection of newly diagnosed atypical meningioma were randomly assigned (1:1) to adjuvant radiotherapy or observation. Randomisation was done using a web-based interface using random variable blocks of sizes two and four, stratified by location (UK or non-UK). Participants assigned to the radiotherapy group received fractionated external-beam intensity-modulated radiotherapy at a total dose of 60 Gy in 30 fractions over 6 weeks. Participants were followed up for a minimum of 4 years. The primary outcome was disease-free survival, defined as time from surgery to MRI-confirmed recurrence or death due to any cause, analysed in all randomly assigned participants in their assigned treatment group. Harms analysis was done in the as-treated population. The trial was registered with ISRCTN, ISRCTN71502099, and has completed. FINDINGS: Between April 28, 2016, and May 21, 2021, 990 patients were assessed for eligibility, 157 of whom were randomly assigned to radiotherapy (n=78) or observation (n=79). Median age was 57·40 years (IQR 49·09-66·93); 84 (54%) participants were female and 73 (46%) were male. At a median follow-up of 64 months (IQR 50-75), meningioma recurrence occurred in 11 (14%) of 78 participants in the radiotherapy group and 24 (30%) of 79 in the observation group. 5-year disease-free survival was 79·9% (95% CI 67·6-87·9) in the radiotherapy group and 64·3% (51·9-74·2) in the observation group (absolute difference 15·6% percentage points [95% CI 0·6-30·5]). Disease-free survival was improved in the radiotherapy group compared with the observation group (hazard ratio 0·51 [95% CI 0·27-0·97]; p=0·0396). Grade 2 or 3 radiation-related serious adverse events occurred in five (8%) of 66 participants in the radiotherapy group, with no treatment-related deaths. INTERPRETATION: Our findings suggest that adjuvant radiotherapy should be considered in patients with atypical meningioma after complete surgical resection of atypical meningioma when the prevention of recurrence is valued higher than the potential delayed adverse effects of radiotherapy. This practice will benefit patients by reducing meningioma recurrence. Decisions should be based on individual discussion with the patient. FUNDING: National Institute for Health and Care Research Health Technology Assessment programme, the European Organisation for Research and Treatment of Cancer Brain Tumour Group and Radiation Oncology Group, and the Heath Research and Medical Research Council of Australia.

articles.title: A multicenter randomized phase III trial of weekly cisplatin chemoradiotherapy versus radiotherapy in elderly patients with head and neck squamous cell carcinoma unfit for high-dose cisplatin: JCOG2405 (ELDER-WEEKLY).
articles.abstract: Chemoradiotherapy (CRT) with high-dose cisplatin (100 mg/m2) is the standard treatment for locally advanced squamous cell carcinoma of the head and neck (SCCHN). However, this regimen is often intolerable in elderly patients because of its toxicity, and the optimal treatment for those unfit for high-dose cisplatin remains unclear. CRT with weekly cisplatin (40 mg/m2) has been developed as a more tolerable alternative and has demonstrated comparable efficacy with reduced toxicity in several trials involving nonelderly patients. We therefore designed a multicenter, randomized phase III trial (JCOG2405) to confirm the superiority of CRT with weekly cisplatin over radiotherapy alone in patients aged ≥70 years with locally advanced SCCHN who are unfit for high-dose cisplatin. The primary endpoint is overall survival. A total of 250 patients from 59 institutions will be enrolled over 5 years. The trial has been registered in the Japan Registry of Clinical Trials (study number: jRCTs031250688).

articles.title: Effect of a Single Subanesthetic Dose of Esketamine on Gastrointestinal Recovery After Laparoscopic Colorectal Cancer Surgery: A Randomized, Outcome-Assessor-Blinded, Placebo-Controlled Trial.
articles.abstract: PURPOSE: Postoperative gastrointestinal dysfunction (POGD) and Postoperative gastrointestinal intolerance (POGI) remain a critical challenge in abdominal surgery, particularly for colorectal cancer patients undergoing laparoscopic procedures. Current evidence suggests anesthetic agents may influence gastrointestinal recovery, yet the impact of esketamine remains underexplored. This trial aimed to investigate whether intraoperative esketamine administration accelerates gastrointestinal function recovery. METHODS: In this single-center, randomized, outcome-assessor -blind trial, 104 patients (aged 18-75, ASA I-III) scheduled for elective laparoscopic colorectal cancer surgery were allocated to receive either intravenous esketamine (0.2 mg/kg) or saline (control) 30 minutes before surgery completion. Primary outcome was time to first flatus; secondary outcomes included I-FEED scores, defecation time, oral intake tolerance, and postoperative complications assessed within seven days after surgery. RESULTS: The esketamine group demonstrated significantly shorter time to first flatus (52 [50.25-53.75] vs 60 [58.59-61.41] hours; P < 0.001) and first defecation (87 [81.96-92.04] vs 95 [92.65-97.35] hours; P = 0.04) compared to controls. I-FEED scores were markedly lower (median 1 [0.25-2] vs 2.5 [1-3]; P < 0.001), with reduced nausea (P = 0.001) and abdominal distension duration (P < 0.001). Esketamine also improved postoperative sleep quality, but did not affect hospitalization costs or length of stay. CONCLUSION: Intraoperative esketamine accelerates gastrointestinal function recovery after laparoscopic colorectal surgery, especially reducing postoperative gastrointestinal intolerance symptoms of nausea and distension while improving early sleep quality. However, no evident benefit was observed in reducing hospital length of stay or patient costs.

articles.title: The conformation-selective PI3Kδ inhibitor roginolisib in patients with advanced or metastatic cancer, including metastatic uveal melanoma: first-in-human clinical trial.
articles.abstract: Phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase delta (PI3Kδ) promotes tumour cell growth directly or indirectly by activating immune-suppressive cells. In contrast to previous PI3Kδ inhibitors, roginolisib is a selective, non-ATP competitive inhibitor, which locks PI3Kδ into an inactive state and causes an allosteric modulation. In a First-in-Human dose study, continuous daily dosing of roginolisib was investigated in patients with solid and haematologic malignancies. In Part A, 24 patients received escalating doses of roginolisib. In Part B, 20 mostly pre-treated metastatic uveal melanoma (mUM) patients received a dose associated with continuous PI3Kδ inhibition of >90%. The primary endpoint was safety, and secondary endpoints included pharmacokinetic (PK) and pharmacodynamic (PD) profile, clinical anti-tumour responses assessments. Exploratory endpoints included immunophenotyping, proteomics, genomics. No Dose Limiting Toxicity or drug related toxicities requiring dose modifications were observed ( ≥ Grade 3 toxicities: 3/44; 6.8%). In mUM, median Overall Survival (mOS) was 20.8 months (data-cut off December 2023) and 18.4 months (data-cut-off February 2026). mOS in mUM patients with Stable Disease at Week 16 ( = Cycle 5) was 28.5 months, while patients who progressed at Week 16 had a median OS of 12.3 months. articles.title: Changes in health literacy following participation in a multidisciplinary primary care intervention for people with chronic pain: a longitudinal cohort study.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Chronic pain is a global public health issue, severely affecting quality of life, functional capacity, and healthcare resources. Effective management requires adequate health literacy, yet limited health literacy is associated with greater pain burden and poorer outcomes. This underlines the need for interventions that can strengthen patients' health literacy skills. Thus, the aim of the present study was to investigate longitudinal changes in health literacy following participation in a multidisciplinary primary care pain management intervention. METHODS: This longitudinal study reports health literacy outcomes from a multidisciplinary, personalized pain management intervention that was developed in accordance with the Medical Research Council framework. Forty-three participants with chronic non-cancer pain completed the full intervention. Health literacy was measured using the Norwegian version of the Health Literacy Questionnaire (HLQ) at baseline, midpoint, and post-intervention. Changes over time were analyzed using paired-sample t-tests. RESULTS: Statistically significant improvements were observed in five HLQ domains from baseline to midpoint and in eight domains from baseline to post-intervention. "Having sufficient information to manage my health" showed the largest increase among Domains 1-5, whereas "Navigating the healthcare system" showed the largest increase among Domains 6-9 and improved significantly across all time-point comparisons. CONCLUSION: Participants demonstrated improvements in several dimensions of health literacy during participation in the intervention, particularly in domains related to having sufficient information to manage health and active self-management. These findings support further investigation of tailored, multidisciplinary approaches to strengthening health literacy among people with chronic pain. TRIAL REGISTRATION: NCT05828121 Date: 04-25-2023.

articles.title: T-cell-redirecting therapies in early relapsed multiple myeloma: a systematic review and network meta-analysis.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Chimeric antigen receptor T cells and bispecific antibodies, are moving from late-line salvage into early relapsed multiple myeloma. Indirect comparisons in heavily pretreated patients have favored cell therapy, but whether that hierarchy holds in early relapse is unknown. METHODS: We analyzed randomized phase 3 trials comparing a T-cell-redirecting therapy against a daratumumab-pomalidomide-dexamethasone-type control after at least one prior line. Pseudo-individual patient time-to-event data were reconstructed from published survival curves. Regimens were compared indirectly in Bayesian network meta-analyses reported under fixed-effect and random-effects assumptions, re-estimated in a frequentist graph-theoretical model. Control-arm dispersion was quantified by random-effects synthesis of median progression-free survival. Overall survival was additionally analyzed as restricted mean survival differences at 24 and 36 months. Safety and a cost-consequence analysis were assessed descriptively (PROSPERO: CRD420261431847). RESULTS: Four trials (2,174 patients) investigating ciltacabtagene autoleucel, teclistamab-daratumumab, and talquetamab-daratumumab with or without pomalidomide were included. Control-arm median progression-free survival spanned 9.9 to 24.4 months (I-squared 91%). Under fixed effects, teclistamab-daratumumab ranked first for progression-free survival (P-score 98%, the mean probability of outranking a competing treatment rather than the probability of being best) and separated from talquetamab-daratumumab (hazard ratio 0.55, 95% credible interval 0.34 to 0.88). Once between-trial heterogeneity was admitted, every contrast crossed unity (versus ciltacabtagene autoleucel 0.62, 0.21 to 1.81). Overall survival was concordant under both models (teclistamab-daratumumab versus ciltacabtagene autoleucel 0.94, 0.55 to 1.62), with restricted mean survival gains over control of 0.7 to 1.6 months at 24 months and rankings between 56% and 70%. Toxicity profiles differed across modalities, although their overall burden cannot be reliably compared across trials. Cost per progression-free month, computed against a population-standardized denominator, was lowest for cilta-cel and converged with the bispecific regimens only under short, fixed treatment durations. CONCLUSIONS: Randomized evidence in early relapse does not establish an efficacy hierarchy among these regimens. Progression-free survival estimates favored teclistamab-daratumumab, but no contrast was robust to plausible between-trial heterogeneity, and equivalence could not be demonstrated. Until comparative data exist, treatment selection cannot rest on efficacy data alone and will be informed by patient- and disease-related factors, toxicity, sequencing, access, and cost.

articles.title: Current status and future perspectives of treatment de-escalation in localized head and neck cancer.
articles.abstract: Head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC) often requires invasive multimodal therapy, including surgery, radiotherapy, and chemotherapy. Although these interventions have improved treatment outcomes, patients frequently experience long-term functional impairment and treatment-related morbidity. Consequently, clinical research has shifted toward treatment de-escalation, a paradigm aimed at preserving quality of life while maintaining oncologic control. This review summarizes the current evidence from prospective clinical trials on de-escalation strategies for HNSCC of the oropharynx, hypopharynx, larynx, and oral cavity, with a focus on radiotherapy-based approaches. Investigators have evaluated several de-escalation strategies, including total radiation dose reduction in definitive chemoradiotherapy, modification or omission of concurrent systemic therapy, de-intensification of prophylactic nodal irradiation, response-adapted treatment de-intensification, and minimally invasive approaches such as transoral surgery with risk-adapted postoperative therapy. These strategies target favorable-risk populations, particularly patients with human papillomavirus-associated oropharyngeal cancer. Although numerous phase II studies have reported encouraging clinical outcomes and acceptable toxicity profiles, definitive evidence supporting the safety and efficacy of de-escalation strategies remains unestablished in large-scale phase III trials. Unwarranted de-escalation for HNSCC should be avoided, particularly for medically fit patients, and promising strategies require validation in phase III trials before routine clinical adoption. Future challenges include prospective validation through clinical trials and the integration of predictive biomarkers to balance the delicate trade-off between toxicity reduction and oncologic safety.

articles.title: Effects of anti-inflammatory dietary education on sleep disturbances among patients with breast cancer undergoing chemotherapy: A randomized controlled trial.
articles.abstract: PURPOSE: This randomized controlled trial evaluated the effects of anti-inflammatory dietary education on sleep disturbances and inflammatory biomarkers in patients with breast cancer undergoing chemotherapy. METHODS: A total of 132 patients with sleep disturbances were randomized to receive either a 12-week anti-inflammatory dietary education program based on the energy-adjusted dietary inflammatory index (E-DII) or usual care. Sleep disturbances were assessed using the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI) at baseline and at 12 weeks. Additional outcomes included inflammatory biomarkers, E-DII scores, and quality of life (QoL). Treatment effects on continuous outcomes were evaluated using linear mixed-effects models (LMMs) under the intention-to-treat principle. The proportions of participants with sleep disturbance (PSQI ≥ 8) at 12 weeks were compared between groups using a completer analysis. RESULTS: Of the 132 participants, 116 (87.9%) completed the 12-week assessment. In the completer analysis, the proportion of participants with sleep disturbance at 12 weeks was significantly lower in the intervention group than in the control group (49.2% vs. 78.9%, P < 0.001). The intervention group demonstrated greater reductions in PSQI (β =  - 2.10; 95% CI: - 3.01, - 1.18; P < 0.001) and E-DII scores (β =  - 1.23; 95% CI: - 1.98, - 0.47; P = 0.002) and improved overall QoL (β = 14.07; 95% CI: 8.61, 19.52; P < 0.001). Furthermore, levels of interleukin-1β, interleukin-6, and C-reactive protein were significantly reduced, whereas interleukin-10 increased (all P < 0.05). CONCLUSION: Anti-inflammatory dietary education reduced sleep disturbances and improved QoL in patients with breast cancer undergoing chemotherapy and was accompanied by favorable changes in inflammatory biomarkers. TRIAL REGISTRATION: ChiCTR2500097053. Registered on 11 February 2025.
